text: Four chapters, four very different ways of building a qubit — and after all of it, the honest answer to which one wins is: none of them, yet. This lesson puts superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic, and neutral-atom hardware side by side.

Superconducting platforms lead on raw gate speed and have the most mature large-scale integration story — but need the heaviest cooling infrastructure, and face real wiring-density limits as they grow.

Trapped-ion systems report some of the best fidelities and get all-to-all connectivity within a single trap — but scale more slowly in raw qubit count, and the bottleneck is scaling one chain or reliably linking multiple traps together.

Photonic systems offer room-temperature operation and a natural fit for networking between processors — but trail on general-purpose fault-tolerant performance, and fight an essentially unrecoverable photon-loss problem.
Neutral-atom systems can genuinely load very large raw numbers of qubits and reconfigure their layout on the fly — but still have real gaps in gate fidelity and atom-loss management.

Each of these is a serious, well-funded, scientifically credible approach, and each has a real, named weakness that hasn't been solved — not a minor footnote. The pattern to carry forward: whenever a company announces a record — most qubits, highest fidelity, fastest gate — ask what's being measured, under what conditions, and what isn't being claimed. A large raw qubit count says little without a fidelity number next to it; a high fidelity on an isolated pair says little about a full connected array.

That closes this chapter. Next: qubit connectivity graphs — the precise tool for describing which qubits on any of these four platforms can actually talk to each other, and why that shapes everything you compile from here on.
